prompt.context: Your friend Carlos wants to invest in a rafting business in California. In addition to the investment, he wants to work as general manager of this business. Carlos has asked you the following questions.
prompt.question:
1. Is the business currently profitable?
2. How much is the business worth?
3. Should Carlos acquire it?

clarifying_info.q: How long is the operating season?
clarifying_info.a: The business is open every day in July and August, and only 2 days per week in May, June, and September. It is closed the rest of the year.

clarifying_info.q: How many boats does the business have?
How many trips does each boat make per day?
clarifying_info.a: Each boat makes on average 20 trips per day.

clarifying_info.q: What is the price per trip?

clarifying_info.a: 4 rafting instructors, each making $15 per hour worked.
General manager salary: $40,000/year; 2 leased vans at $5,000/van/year; insurance: $8,000/year; overhead: $2,000/year.

clarifying_info.q: What discount rate should we use for the valuation?
What valuation method should we use?

framework: Map the revenue structure: boats × trips/day × price × operating days
Calculate operating days carefully — seasonal schedule means different day counts per month
Map and categorize all costs: variable (labor) vs. fixed (GM salary, vans, insurance, overhead)
Calculate annual profit = revenue − total costs
Value the business using perpetuity: CF / r
Assess qualitative acquisition factors: risk, growth assumptions, opportunity cost

questions.guidance: Candidate must first determine total operating days. July + August = 62 days (open every day). May, June, September = ~13 weeks × 2 days = 26 days (casebook uses 24). Total ≈ 84 days. Revenue = price × trips per boat per day × number of boats × days.

steps: Operating days: July (31) + August (31) = 62 days; May, June, September at 2 days/week × ~4 weeks each ≈ 24 days → total = 84 days

questions.guidance: Variable cost is labor — 4 instructors working each operating day. Assume 8 hours per day.
Sum all fixed line items: GM salary, van leases, insurance, overhead. A strong candidate identifies insurance as a non-obvious but significant cost in a risky outdoor business.

questions.prompt: Is the business currently profitable? Calculate annual profit.
questions.guidance: Total costs ≈ $100,000; revenue = $168,000. Business is profitable.

questions.prompt: How much is the business worth? (Question 2)
questions.guidance: Use operating profit as a proxy for cash flow (ignoring taxes, working capital, capex). Assume zero growth. Apply perpetuity formula CF/r.
No additional numerical info is given. Candidate should reason qualitatively about risks and strategic fit.

brainstorming.prompt: What qualitative factors and risks should Carlos consider before deciding to acquire the business?

categories.name: Business Risk
ideas: Revenue is highly weather-dependent — bad seasons can significantly reduce cash flows
Seasonal concentration in 3 months means one bad summer wipes out the year
Safety and liability exposure in an outdoor adventure business

categories.name: Valuation Assumptions
ideas: Zero-growth assumption may undervalue a growing outdoor recreation market
Perpetuity assumes the business runs indefinitely — equipment and lease renewals not modeled
Discount rate of 10% may not fully capture the operating risk of a seasonal business

categories.name: Opportunity Cost
ideas: Are there better uses for the capital at the same risk level?
Carlos will also forgo other income by taking the GM role — his opportunity cost of time matters

categories.name: Strategic / Operational
ideas: Carlos has no stated experience running an adventure business
Could revenue be grown by adding boats, extending the season, or raising prices?
Are there competitors in the California rafting market that could erode margins?

categories.name: Financial
ideas: Purchase price vs. $680,000 estimated value — is the asking price fair?
Working capital needs: revenue is seasonal but costs (GM salary, insurance, leases) are year-round

recommendation: The business is currently profitable at ~$68,000/year and valued at approximately $680,000 on a perpetuity basis
Whether Carlos should acquire depends heavily on the asking price relative to $680,000 and his risk tolerance
risks: Revenue is weather-dependent and highly seasonal — one poor summer materially impacts annual cash flow
The zero-growth, no-tax perpetuity model likely overstates value; a risk-adjusted or finite-horizon model would be more conservative
Insurance and liability exposure in rafting are substantial and could increase
next_steps: Confirm the asking price and compare to the $680,000 valuation estimate
Conduct due diligence on historical revenue/cash flow stability and any past insurance claims
Assess whether Carlos has or can hire the operational expertise to manage a seasonal outdoor business
Explore growth options (additional boats, extended season, pricing power) to stress-test the zero-growth assumption
